title: Sachem Warawakmy of the Setauket
summary: Warawakmy was a mid-seventeenth-century Setauket sachem named in the April 14, 1655 Setauket land deed.
content:
Warawakmy was a mid-seventeenth-century Setauket sachem named in the April 14, 1655 Setauket land deed. The surviving record does not preserve a full account of his life or establish his birth or death dates.

The deed record connects him with North Shore land between Stony Brook and the Peconic headwaters, but it does not preserve a full personal biography.12

Historical Context

Warawakmy is described as the Setauket chief who, with fourteen other Native men, sold a thirty-two-square-mile tract on the North Shore to English settlers.1

Later records point to a Setauket sachem named Gie who apparently succeeded Warawakmy, so the history does not extend Warawakmy's leadership into the later seventeenth century without evidence.3

References

  1. John A. Strong, The Unkechaug Indians of Eastern Long Island: A History, pp. 41, 69.
  2. John A. Strong, The Algonquian Peoples of Long Island from Earliest Times to 1700.
  3. William Wallace Tooker, Indian Place-Names on Long Island and Islands Adjacent.
why_this_matters: Warawakmy places Setauket history within Native homelands and leadership before English town formation. His brief record should be named clearly without pretending colonial sources preserved a complete life story.
